name: Hypermanganesaemia with dystonia
aliases: hypermanganesaemia with dystonia, polycythaemia and cirrhosis

reference.source: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics / Journal of Inherited Metabolic Disease
clinicalPearls: An inherited manganese-overload disorder presenting with dystonia and a parkinsonian gait, sometimes described as a high-stepping cock-walk
Two forms exist: SLC30A10 deficiency (type 1) causing manganese retention with liver disease, and SLC39A14 deficiency (type 2) causing childhood-onset dystonia usually without hepatic involvement
Whole-blood manganese is markedly elevated, and this should be measured whenever unexplained dystonia is combined with polycythaemia or liver disease
Brain MRI shows symmetrical T1-weighted hyperintensity in the basal ganglia (and often the white matter, pituitary, and cerebellum) from paramagnetic manganese deposition
Polycythaemia arises because manganese stimulates erythropoietin production; iron studies typically show low ferritin with high total iron-binding capacity
In SLC30A10 disease hepatic manganese accumulation drives fibrosis and cirrhosis
Treatment centres on chelation to enhance urinary manganese excretion, dietary manganese restriction, and iron supplementation to competitively reduce manganese uptake
Early recognition and chelation can arrest or improve neurological and hepatic disease
reference.pathophysiology: This group of disorders reflects disrupted whole-body manganese homeostasis. SLC30A10 encodes a manganese efflux transporter that exports manganese from hepatocytes into bile and from enterocytes and neurons; its loss causes manganese to accumulate in the liver and brain. SLC39A14 encodes an importer required for hepatic manganese uptake and biliary clearance; its loss paradoxically raises circulating manganese and drives brain deposition while sparing the liver. Excess manganese is neurotoxic to the basal ganglia, producing extrapyramidal features that resemble manganese-induced parkinsonism, and it deposits as a paramagnetic species giving the characteristic T1 basal-ganglia signal. Manganese also upregulates erythropoietin, explaining the polycythaemia, and interacts with iron handling, producing a low-ferritin state.
additionalDifferentials: Wilson disease and other inherited metal-storage disorders
Acquired manganese toxicity (parenteral nutrition, environmental or occupational exposure, chronic liver failure)
Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation syndromes
Primary polycythaemia (JAK2-related) when the neurological picture is overlooked
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI looking for T1 basal-ganglia hyperintensity
Full blood count for polycythaemia and iron studies (ferritin, transferrin saturation)
Liver function tests and hepatic imaging or elastography
Molecular genetic testing of SLC30A10 and SLC39A14
24-hour urinary manganese excretion to guide and monitor chelation
redFlags: Rapidly progressive dystonia or gait failure in a child or young adult
Decompensated liver disease or established cirrhosis in SLC30A10 disease
Deterioration despite treatment, prompting review of chelation adequacy
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on early diagnosis; chelation and manganese restriction can stabilise or improve neurological and hepatic disease, but delayed treatment risks fixed dystonia and, in SLC30A10 disease, progressive cirrhosis.
pitfalls: Failing to measure blood manganese in unexplained dystonia with polycythaemia or liver disease
Misreading the T1 basal-ganglia signal as hepatic encephalopathy of unknown cause
Attributing the polycythaemia to a primary myeloproliferative disorder
Delaying chelation and iron supplementation while awaiting genetic confirmation
references: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
management: Reduce the manganese burden with chelation using intravenous disodium calcium edetate, monitoring urinary manganese excretion to guide treatment courses
Give oral iron supplementation to compete with manganese uptake and lower its absorption and deposition, particularly in SLC30A10 disease
Restrict dietary and environmental manganese exposure
Treat dystonia symptomatically with agents such as anticholinergics, baclofen or botulinum toxin injections, supported by physiotherapy
Monitor whole-blood manganese, full blood count for polycythaemia, iron studies, and liver function with hepatic imaging or elastography in SLC30A10 disease
Consider liver transplantation for end-stage hepatic disease in SLC30A10 deficiency
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance and coordinate metabolic, neurology and hepatology care
